Whole
hōle
a. (entire, complete; also sound, healed; rendering Hebrew kol, Greek holos and hugies)
From the Saxon hal, sound, well — the same root that gives hale, heal, and holy. English preserves in one word what Scripture holds together: to be whole is to be unbroken, and to be healed is to be made whole again.

Biblical Definition

Whole carries two senses in the Authorized Version that turn out to be one. It means entire, the sum and not a part: “Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man” (Ecclesiastes 12:13). And it means sound, unbroken, restored — the word for healing. Our Lord uses the second sense with deliberate irony: “They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick” (Matthew 9:12), spoken to men who were not whole and did not know it. To the woman with the issue of blood he says, “Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague” (Mark 5:34) — and the word covers both her body and her standing, for she had been cut off by the law of uncleanness and is now sent away in peace. Paul gathers the senses into a prayer for the whole man: “I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 5:23). Scripture knows nothing of a soul saved out of a body discarded; the redemption in view is of the entire man, and it is completed at the resurrection.

Webster 1828 Definition

Entire, complete, all of a thing; and also sound or healed. The English word carries both senses because Scripture does — the healed man is the man made whole again.

expand to see more

WHOLE, a. hole. [Sax. hal, sound, whole; the root of heal and hale.] All; total; containing the total amount or number; as, the whole earth; the whole matter.

2. Complete; entire; not defective or imperfect; as, a whole duty.

3. Sound; not broken; as, a whole vessel.

4. Restored to health; healed; as, thy faith hath made thee whole, Mark 5.

5. In Scripture, the whole man, spirit and soul and body, 1 Thess. 5.

Key Scripture

Ecclesiastes 12:13 — "Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man."

Matthew 9:12 — "But when Jesus heard that, he said unto them, They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick."

Mark 5:34 — "And he said unto her, Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague."

1 Thessalonians 5:23 — "And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ."

Modern Corruption

Wholeness has been taken over as a therapeutic goal — self-integration, feeling entire. Scripture's wholeness is made, not achieved, and it comes to those who first admit they are not whole.

expand to see more

The modern vocabulary of wholeness locates the problem in fragmentation and the cure in integration: a man is to gather up his parts and become entire by his own inner work. Scripture agrees that man is broken and disagrees entirely about the remedy. The woman in Mark 5 did not integrate herself; she touched Christ's garment and was made whole, and the passive voice is the doctrine. Matthew 9:12 exposes the harder problem — the men who most needed the physician were the ones convinced they were already whole, and self-assessment is precisely the faculty sin has damaged.

The recovery runs through 1 Thessalonians 5:23. Biblical wholeness is not psychological unity but the preservation of the entire man — spirit and soul and body — blameless unto the coming of Christ, which means it is eschatological and God does it. That has two consequences worth holding. It forbids the false spirituality that treats the body as incidental to salvation, since the body is named in the prayer. And it relieves the believer of an impossible project, because the God of peace who sanctifies is the one who will also perform it: faithful is he that calleth you, who also will do it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kol is all or the whole; shalem is whole in the sense of complete and at peace, cognate with shalom. Greek holos is entire and hugies is sound or healthy, the word behind made whole.

expand to see more

Hebrew kol (H3605) — all, the whole, every; the ordinary word for totality.

Hebrew shalem (H8003) — whole, complete, at peace; kin to shalom, which is wholeness rather than mere quiet.

Greek holos (G3650) — whole, entire; behind your whole spirit and soul and body.

Greek hugies (G5199) — sound, healthy, whole; the word for a healed man, giving English hygiene.

Greek sozo (G4982) — to save, to make whole; the same verb serves for healing the body and saving the soul.

Usage

"Of the sum of a man's obligation: fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man (Ecclesiastes 12:13)."

"Of those who think they need no physician: they that be whole need not a physician (Matthew 9:12)."

"Of the entire man preserved to the last day: your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless (1 Thessalonians 5:23)."
